EAQ48.brief: Baked lighting is light that Unreal calculates once in the editor and stores in textures called lightmaps. A mesh that uses baked lighting needs a special UV channel, the lightmap UV, where no two faces share the same space. Projects that use Lumen calculate light while the game runs and do not need lightmaps at all. In this quest you find out which kind of lighting a project uses and look at the lightmap settings of one prop.
checklist: Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open Project Settings, then Engine, then Rendering. Note whether Dynamic Global Illumination is set to Lumen, and whether Allow Static Lighting is turned on.

Open a prop whose name starts with SM_ in the Static Mesh Editor, for example SM_Chair from the Props folder of the Starter Content. In the Details panel, expand LOD0 and then Build Settings. Find Generate Lightmap UVs, Min Lightmap Resolution, Source Lightmap Index and Destination Lightmap Index.
Set Min Lightmap Resolution to 64 and click Apply Changes. Then use the UV button in the toolbar to view the lightmap UV channel.
Under General Settings, check that Lightmap Resolution and Lightmap Coordinate Index match the channel you generated.
Write three lines that answer these questions: does this project bake its lighting or use Lumen, and does this prop need a lightmap UV at all?

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Make a material named M_Blend2 that blends two textures from the Starter Content with a Lerp node, and use the alpha of a Vertex Color node to control the blend. Place a prop with many vertices in the level, for example SM_Rock from the Starter Content, and apply the material to it.
Enter Mesh Paint mode. Choose the Vertex Weight paint method, and set Texture Weight Type to Alpha (Two Textures).
Set Paint Texture Weight Index to the second texture and paint dirt or moss on the lower part of the prop. Use Ctrl + [ and Ctrl + ] to make the brush smaller or larger.
Use Color View Mode to look at the Alpha channel. This shows you exactly where you painted.
Click To LODs so that the paint is copied to all LOD levels, which are the simpler versions of the mesh used at a distance. Then click Save.
Duplicate the prop. Use Copy on the painted prop and Paste on the new copy to move the paint across.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Make a small test level that has a floor, a sloped ramp (a cube that you rotate) and a table mesh, such as the table from the Props folder of the Starter Content.

In the toolbar of the Level Viewport, enable Surface Snapping and Rotate to Surface Normal. Drag five small props, for example from the Props folder of the Starter Content, onto the ramp and see how they tilt to match the slope.
Set Surface Offset to 5 and place one prop, so you can see the small gap it creates. Then set Surface Offset back to 0.
Select a prop that floats in the air and press End. Watch it drop to the nearest surface below it.
Hold V and drag one prop so that its pivot snaps to a vertex of the table. A vertex is a corner point of a mesh.
In Modeling Mode, open Xform, then Edit Pivot, and move the pivot of a prop to Bottom. Then place the prop again with surface snapping.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. In a level, arrange a small group of props that uses only Static Meshes. For example, use a table, two chairs and a lamp from the Props folder of the Starter Content.
Select all the actors and right-click one of them. Go to Level and choose Create Packed Level Actor. Set Pivot Type to Center Min Z, click Ok, and save it as BP_Kit_TableSet.
Drag three more copies of BP_Kit_TableSet into the level and rotate them.
Edit the Packed Level Actor: click Edit in the Outliner and move one chair. Then commit the change and see all copies update.
Select another group of the same kind, and this time use Create Level Instance to make a Level Instance. Note how it looks different in the Outliner.
Use the Break option on one instance and see the original actors come back.
Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a small level that has two rooms or two clearly different areas. The level of the template is fine.
Place a Post Process Volume and name it PPV_Global. In Post Process Volume Settings, turn on Infinite Extent (Unbound) so it affects the whole level, and keep Priority at 0.
Place a second Post Process Volume around one room and name it PPV_Room. Leave Infinite Extent off and set Priority to 100.
In PPV_Room, override one setting that is easy to see. For example, open Color Grading, then Global, and set Saturation to 0.2.
Set Blend Radius on PPV_Room to 0. Play from the viewport and walk in and out of the room. Then set Blend Radius to 1000, walk again, and note the difference.
Set Blend Weight on PPV_Room to 0.5 and look at the room again.
Open Project Settings, then Rendering, then Default Settings, and find where the post process defaults for the whole project are stored. Do not change them.

Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a level that has a dark interior and a bright exterior. If you do not have one, build a closed box from cubes with one open door in a new Basic level.

Place a Post Process Volume and turn on Infinite Extent (Unbound), or use the global volume your level already has. In it, open Lens, then Exposure, and set Metering Mode to Auto Exposure Histogram. In the viewport, turn on Show > Visualize > HDR (Eye Adaptation) and watch the graph as you move from dark to bright.
Override Speed Up and Speed Down. Try Speed Up 10 with Speed Down 1, and then the reverse. Note which one feels more like real eyes.
Override Exposure Compensation. Try -1 and then +1, and note what happens to the image.

Place a Cine Camera Actor and pilot it with Ctrl+Shift+P, which means you look through it. In the camera's own post process settings, set Metering Mode to Manual and turn on Apply Physical Camera Exposure.
Set ISO, Shutter Speed and Aperture on the camera until the interior looks right. Write the three values down.
Turn on Local Exposure in the volume. Use Show > Visualization > Local Exposure to see where it works.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Pick one camera view in a level that already has lighting, such as the level of the template, and save it as a camera bookmark with Ctrl+1. Take a screenshot before you change anything, so you have the ungraded picture.

Place a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on, or use the one your level already has. In it, open Color Grading, then Temperature. Keep Temperature Type on White Balance. Move Temp up and down and note which direction makes the image warm.
Adjust Tint a little to remove any green or magenta color that covers the whole image.
Open Color Grading, then Global, and do the main work here. Set Saturation, Contrast and Gamma until the image has the mood you want.
Use a small amount of Offset under Global to make the shadows lighter or darker.
Only now change Shadows or Highlights, and only if one part of the image still needs help.
Take the graded screenshot from the same camera.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. In a level that has lighting, such as the level of the template, place a few spheres with different colors and one with a strong emissive material, which is a material that glows. Take a reference screenshot.

Place a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on, or use the one your level already has. In it, open the Film category. Override Slope and move it up and down. Note which direction makes the image darker.
Override Toe and Shoulder, one at a time. Watch what happens to the darkest and the brightest areas of the image.
Raise the emissive brightness of one sphere by a large amount. Watch how its color changes as it gets very bright.
Put Slope, Toe and Shoulder back to their default values. Write one line about when the Film settings should be changed.
This step is optional. Open Color Grading, then Misc, and set Tone Curve Amount and Expand Gamut to 0 to see the image without the tone curve. Then restore the values.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. In a new level, build a small room from cubes. Give the floor a material named M_Floor_Shiny with Roughness 0.1, and add a few colored props. Put one tall prop just outside the camera view.
Place a Post Process Volume with Infinite Extent (Unbound) turned on. In it, open Reflections and set Method to Lumen. Take a screenshot. Then change Max Roughness To Trace and watch the floor.
Set Method to Screen Space Reflections. Look at the floor near the edge of the screen and find where the prop that is outside the view disappears from the reflection. Take a screenshot.
Place a Sphere Reflection Capture in the room, and change Method to None. Observe how the capture alone reflects the room. Take a screenshot.

Open Project Settings, then Rendering, then Reflections, and turn on Support global clip plane for Planar Reflections. Restart the editor, and then place a Planar Reflection Actor on the floor. Take a screenshot.
Write one line for each method that says what it can reflect and what it costs.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and work in any lit level. Create a material named M_Blend_Test with a colored Base Color. This is the opaque starting point that you copy in the next steps. Place four spheres in front of a wall, one for each blend mode you will try.

Duplicate the material and name the copy M_Blend_Masked. Set its Blend Mode to Masked. Connect a pattern with clear light and dark areas to Opacity Mask, for example a striped or checker texture, or a Checker Pattern node, and try two different Opacity Mask Clip Values. Apply it to the first sphere.

Duplicate M_Blend_Test again and name the copy M_Blend_Translucent. Set its Blend Mode to Translucent and connect a gradient to Opacity, for example one channel of a Texture Coordinate node. Apply it to the second sphere.

Duplicate again to make M_Blend_Additive, with Blend Mode Additive, and M_Blend_Modulate, with Blend Mode Modulate, set to Unlit, and with the color connected to Emissive. Apply them to the third and fourth sphere. Move two spheres so that they overlap, and look at the area where they overlap.

On M_Blend_Translucent, open the Translucency section in the Details panel. Place a Point Light nearby and compare these three Lighting Mode values: Volumetric NonDirectional, Surface TranslucencyVolume and Surface ForwardShading.
Take one screenshot with all four blend modes visible, and one screenshot with the three lighting modes side by side.

Open a project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Create a material named M_Glass. Set Blend Mode to Translucent. Under Translucency, set Lighting Mode to Surface TranslucencyVolume so that the Refraction pin appears.

Add a Scalar Parameter named Opacity with the value 0.3 and connect it to Opacity. Add a Scalar Parameter named IOR with the value 1.52. Use a Fresnel node to drive a Lerp between 1.0 at the center and IOR at the edges, and connect the result to Refraction.

Create a Material Instance named MI_Glass and apply it to a sphere in front of a textured wall, for example a cube with a brick material from the Starter Content. Try IOR 1.0, 1.33, 1.52 and 2.42, and take a screenshot of each.
Add a Normal Map texture parameter and connect it to Normal. The texture T_Water_N from Starter Content works well. See how the refraction breaks up.
Find Refraction Depth Bias in the Details panel of the material. Try a small value while you look at a close object through the glass.
This step is optional. Duplicate the material as M_Glass_Thin, and set Shading Model to Thin Translucent and Lighting Mode to Surface ForwardShading. Compare the highlights.

EAQ59.brief: Substrate is the newer material system in Unreal Engine 5. Instead of the classic inputs such as Base Color and Metallic, you describe a surface with a building block called a Slab, and you connect it to one input named Front Material. Here F0 is the amount of light a surface reflects when you look straight at it: low for plastic, high for metal. In this quest you check if a project uses Substrate and build two simple Slab materials so that the system is familiar when you meet it.
EAQ59.done_when: Send a screenshot of the M_Substrate_Test graph with the Slab connected to Front Material, a screenshot of the two spheres side by side, and the two lines that you wrote in step 6.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Open Project Settings, then Rendering, and check whether Substrate materials is enabled in the project. Write down what you found, and also the GBuffer Format.
Create a material named M_Substrate_Test. If Substrate is on, add a Substrate Slab node and connect it to the Front Material input on the root node.
Set Diffuse Albedo to a color, F0 to 0.04 (which is a plastic) and Roughness to 0.3. Apply the material to a sphere.
Duplicate the material. Set F0 to a bright color (which is a metal) and Diffuse Albedo to black. Apply it to a second sphere and compare the two.

Open any old material that does not use Substrate, for example a copy of a material from the template. Right-click the root node and read the Convert to Substrate option. Do NOT convert a material that other people share. Use a copy instead.
Write two lines: one that says what a Slab is made of, and one that says what happens to a converted material if Substrate is turned off.
